Excluded, decided on #1774. Reached via the Dataverse API (doi:10.7910/DVN/1KDJTZ) -- access is not the problem. The record holds a single file with 15 columns: Age, Education Level, Nationality and bare CFC1-CFC12. No codebook, no questionnaire, no wording anywhere, and the IRW dictionary row is empty (no Description, no Reference, no DOI). The only evidence tying the table to the Consideration of Future Consequences scale is the column prefix. Shipping it would mean assigning canonical CFC wording (Strathman et al. 1994) to CFC1-CFC12 by assumed publication order with nothing in the record stating that order, no author or paper to check against, and no statistical route since all 12 items share one 1-5 scale -- so a wrong ordering would be undetectable and entirely plausible, the gilbert_meta_35 failure mode. Weaker than the galindo_2023_* tables excluded earlier, which at least had a named study and a code-to-subscale map. Retryable if a paper for this dataset ever surfaces.

Held from batch_021 under #1831, not excluded -- retryable if a fuller COVIDiSTRESS Round II codebook surfaces. SOURCE CORRECTION, raised and applied under #1831 on 2026-09-04: the IRW dictionary attributed all eleven ecps_sahm_2024_* tables to Sahm, Burghart & Mier's German ERQ-S validation, which is wrong. The ERQ-S is a 10-item two-factor measure with none of these item codes; the data are the COVIDiSTRESS Global Survey Round II, whose cleaned file Final_COVIDiSTRESS_Vol2_cleaned.csv is hosted in the ERQ-S OSF project alongside its own files, and every item code in all eight tables is a column of it. The questionnaire is osf.io/36tsd 'Measured Variables.xlsx' and osf.io/vxuf4 'MainStudy_CriticalMeasures.xlsx' (CC-BY 4.0). Five sibling tables (ia, distrust, identity, moral, sscd) shipped in batch_021. This table is 11 items, 6 resilience and 5 uncertainty. Resilience maps cleanly: the questionnaire lists exactly 6 statements and the codes are resilience_1-6. Uncertainty does not: the codes are uncertainty_1-5 but the questionnaire lists only 4 statements ('I always want to know what the future has in store for me', 'When it's time to act, uncertainty paralyses me', 'I can't stand being taken by surprise', 'Unforeseen events upset me greatly'), and the row between the first and second holds only a stray '0' in the Question column, so no fifth item is hiding there. With 4 texts for 5 codes, listing order does not say which code is unlabelled, so any assignment beyond uncertainty_1 would be wrong for an unknown subset. Since validate_items.R requires the shipped item set to match live data exactly, a partial table is not an option, so the whole table is held. Retry needs the fifth uncertainty item, most likely from the published data descriptor rather than these two workbooks.

The first two map cleanly on count and order. The 14 secondary stressors do not. The questionnaire spreads them over six conditionally displayed blocks -- general 4, relationship 1, occupation 4, student 2, children 2, others 1 -- which totals exactly 14, so document order is the obvious mapping. The data contradict it: under that order the four occupation items would be indices 6-9, but n runs 9,905 and 9,623 for indices 6 and 7 and then 6 and 8 rows for indices 8 and 9, while indices 10-11 have ~1,140 and 12-13 have ~3,200. Two occupation items cannot be near-empty while their block-mates are among the most answered, so the index-to-block assignment is not document order. Note also that 'Sharing a workspace with others' appears verbatim in both the occupation and student blocks, which is a plausible route to a Qualtrics collapse. Held rather than shipped on an order inference the data refute. PSS-10 and primary_stressors could ship as a partial table if the item-set gate ever allowed one.
